question: A patient with an indwelling urinary catheter for 5 days develops fever and pyuria. Urine culture grows a Gram-negative rod. Which of the following organisms is MOST commonly associated with Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI)?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. E. coli is the most common cause of CAUTI, accounting for roughly 25–30 % of cases. Its fimbrial adhesins facilitate attachment to catheter biofilms and uroepithelium, and it originates from the patient's own bowel flora.

Incorrect. CoNS — especially S. epidermidis — are the leading cause of Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI), not CAUTI. Their ability to form biofilms on intravascular plastic makes them catheter-relevant, but for central venous lines, not urinary catheters.

Incorrect. S. pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) causes pharyngitis and skin infections but is not a recognised cause of CAUTI. Catheter-associated UTIs are caused by organisms that colonise the perineum — predominantly Gram-negative enteric bacilli.

Incorrect. M. tuberculosis can cause genitourinary TB via haematogenous spread, but this is not a device-associated HAI. CAUTI organisms ascend along the catheter from the perineal flora — E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Candida and Enterococcus.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the HAI-types table. CAUTI organisms ascend from the perineal/bowel flora via the catheter — E. coli is the most common, followed by Klebsiella and Pseudomonas.
E. coli is the leading CAUTI organism. Remember: CAUTI pathogens originate from bowel flora — E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus and Candida top the list.
